title: Rivers of living water (John 7:25–52)
hook: on the great day of the feast he cries: let anyone thirsty come

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot, huts with roofs of branches, and a teacher judged by appearances. Your line was judge not by appearance.

A golden pitcher, a pool, and a procession at dawn. According to Jewish tradition written down in the Mishnah, on the mornings of the Feast of Tabernacles a priest walked down to the pool of Siloam, filled a golden pitcher, and carried it back up to the temple, with crowds and music. At the altar, he poured the water out. In a dry land waiting for the winter rains, that poured-out water meant something. Now it's the last day of the feast, the greatest day. And in the middle of the crowds, Jesus stands up and shouts.

"In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." Then: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Belly is the old, literal word. Here it means the deepest inside of a person, which is why some modern translations say heart. And there's a puzzle: whose heart? The sentence can be read two ways: rivers flowing out of the believer, or out of Jesus himself, for anyone who comes and drinks. Readers have taken it both ways. John explains in the next verse: Jesus was speaking about the Spirit, which those who believed would receive. A woman at a well heard about living water. A crowd heard about bread. Now, at a festival of water, Jesus offers rivers. And the crowd splits. Some say he's the prophet, some the Christ. Others say the Christ can't come from Galilee. Officers sent to arrest him come back empty-handed. Why didn't you bring him? "Never man spake like this man." And one quiet voice on the council speaks up: Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter three. Shouldn't we hear a man before judging him? He's beginning to come out of the dark.

If you have a glass of water near you, hold it; if not, picture one, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, pipes under your street, the people who keep them working. Take a slow sip and notice that your body needed it, even if you didn't feel thirsty. If you pray, give thanks for the water; if you don't, give thanks for the glass in your hand.
Belly. The old, literal word for the deepest inside of a person: out of it, Jesus said, would flow rivers of living water.
Your line: out of the heart, rivers. The old word was belly. That's day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Christians often read this passage at Pentecost, connecting the rivers of living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit; many also connect it with baptism.

chat.meaning: Belly is the old, literal word for a person's deepest inside, and John explains Jesus was speaking about the Spirit.

Mishnah.meaning: an early written collection of Jewish tradition

Siloam.meaning: the pool the priest drew water from

Feast of Tabernacles.meaning: Sukkot, the Jewish feast of booths

Nicodemus.meaning: the teacher who came by night, now on the council

notes: Water-drawing ceremony from Siloam with a golden flagon: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (and 5:1 on the rejoicing). Whether it was done on all seven days, and whether the 'great day' is the seventh or eighth, is debated. Confirm.
Two punctuations of 7:37–38 (believer-centered vs. Christ-centered) both have early church support. Confirm.
'Teachers usually sat to teach' (cf. Luke 4:20, Matthew 5:1): confirm generalization.
Index carry says 'heart'; KJV has 'belly'. Script explains both.
